scenes.title: Chronos Transit Engine
scenes.narration: This is the Chronos Transit Engine. It takes a star's brightness over time from NASA's TESS, Kepler and K2 missions, searches it for the small, regular dips a planet makes when it crosses its star, measures that planet, and decides whether the dip is a planet, an eclipsing binary, or noise. Let's walk through the whole system.

scenes.title: Current conditions at a glance
scenes.narration: The overview is the home page. Here the archive holds one hundred and five target stars and one hundred and seventeen completed runs. Thirty-seven signals were sent to vetting as planet candidates, thirty-five were flagged as false positives, and forty-nine are waiting for a human decision. On the right is the classifier's score, and where the runs came from.

scenes.title: Queue, activity and throughput
scenes.narration: Further down, the overview lists the vetting queue, the most recent activity, and how long each pipeline stage takes. The period search and the refined analysis do most of the work. Below that, a chart shows runs and candidates per day, beside the breakdown of every completed run.

scenes.title: Start with a star
scenes.narration: Every analysis starts here. Name any TESS, Kepler or K2 target and the engine fetches its light curve from NASA's MAST archive. You can also upload your own data as a CSV file, or inject a simulated planet. The host star's properties are filled in from the catalogue, and the list on the right shows each step the pipeline will run.

focus.label: Name a TESS, Kepler or K2 target
Or upload a CSV, or simulate

scenes.title: The verdict, and the planet it measured
scenes.narration: This is a finished run: the star WASP-12, from one sector of TESS data. The engine gives a ninety-four percent planet probability from twenty-one transits, and sends it to the vetting queue. On the right are the measurements: an orbit of just over one day, a dip of nearly one and a half percent, and a planet about twenty-three times the radius of Earth.

scenes.title: False-positive checks and the NASA cross-match
scenes.narration: Next come the false-positive checks. Odd and even transits are compared, the engine looks for a second dip half an orbit later, and it checks whether the star's image shifts during transit. Here no flags are raised. The run is then matched against the NASA Exoplanet Archive, which confirms this is WASP-12 b at the same period. A reviewer can confirm or reject it, and download the archived data.

focus.label: Matches WASP-12 b in NASA's archive

scenes.title: A visual model, drawn to scale
scenes.narration: The visual model shows what the star and its companion are doing. On the left, the planet crosses the star's disc as seen from Earth, with the orbit from above, all drawn to scale and animated. On the right, the fitted transit is laid over the observed data, with the leftover scatter plotted underneath.

scenes.title: The evidence, plot by plot
scenes.narration: Three plots carry the evidence. Odd and even transits overlap, as they should for a planet. Half an orbit later there is no deep second eclipse. And the depth of each transit holds steady. Below, the companion is drawn beside Earth, Neptune and Jupiter, and its orbit beside Mercury's: forty-six times closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun.

focus.label: To scale with the Solar System

scenes.title: The classifier at work
scenes.narration: This diagram is the classifier, drawn with this run's own data. The folded light curve goes in on the left, through two branches of a neural network: one sees the whole orbit, the other sees the transit up close. The network alone said fifty-nine percent planet. The vetting evidence then lifted the final answer to ninety-four. Below, every transit is stacked, next to a plot of what the network paid attention to.

focus.label: Two branches: whole orbit and close-up

scenes.title: Light curve, periodogram and folded transit
scenes.narration: Here is the raw material: more than sixteen thousand brightness measurements across twenty-six days, with dashed lines marking each predicted transit. The periodogram below shows the search over fifteen thousand trial periods, with one clear peak. Beside it, all the transits are folded on top of each other, which is exactly what the classifier is given.

scenes.title: An audit trail for every stage
scenes.narration: Every run ends with its audit trail. Each stage, from ingest to archive, writes a timestamped record, and every record is chained to the one before it with a cryptographic hash, so nothing can be changed quietly afterwards. You can verify the chain or download the log from here.

scenes.title: Every host star in the archive
scenes.narration: The targets page lists every star the engine has looked at. You can filter by mission, or search by name or catalogue number. Each row shows the star's temperature, radius and mass, with the latest period, radius and verdict found for it.

focus.label: Each star, with its latest result

scenes.title: One star, in context
scenes.narration: Open a star to see it in context. WASP-12 is nearly fourteen hundred light-years from Earth. The light we see from it tonight left in the year six hundred and thirty-three, and Voyager 1 would need almost twenty-five million years to get there. Underneath are all the runs made on this star.

focus.label: Every run made on this star

scenes.title: The pipeline ledger
scenes.narration: The runs page is the ledger of everything the pipeline has done. Filter by status or by verdict, search for a target or a run number, and download the full list as a spreadsheet. The median run here took thirty-eight seconds.

scenes.title: A human makes the final call
scenes.narration: The engine never has the last word. Every strong signal lands in the vetting queue, where a person confirms it or marks it as a false positive. Forty-nine signals are waiting here. Confirmed candidates can then be exported for follow-up.

focus.label: Confirm, or mark a false positive

scenes.title: Detections among the known planets
scenes.narration: The atlas places the engine's detections among the planets we already know. The faint points are nearly five thousand confirmed transiting planets, plotted by orbital period and size. The engine's own candidates, eclipsing binaries and signals needing review are drawn on top, with a guide to reading the diagram on the right.

scenes.title: The map begins at home
scenes.narration: The map shows where the known planets really are. It opens on our own Solar System, drawn to scale, with the dashed line tracing Voyager 1 on its way out. From here you can zoom from Earth's orbit all the way to the whole Galaxy, or jump straight to a place using the shortcuts above the map.

scenes.title: The neighbourhood, and how far it really is
scenes.narration: Zoom out and the nearest stars with planets appear. Select one, here TRAPPIST-1, and the panel tells you how far away it is. Forty light-years. The light you would see tonight left in nineteen eighty-five, and Voyager 1 would take seven hundred thousand years to arrive. Its seven known planets are listed underneath.

scenes.title: Seven orbits and a liquid-water zone
scenes.narration: Zoom all the way in on TRAPPIST-1 and its seven orbits appear, drawn to scale, with the shaded band where liquid water could exist. The whole system is tiny. Light crosses this view in under two minutes.

focus.label: Seven orbits and the liquid-water zone

scenes.title: Every known planetary system
scenes.narration: Pull back to the whole Galaxy, and every one of the four thousand eight hundred known planetary systems fits in a small patch around the Sun. The spike is the Kepler telescope's field of view. The streak on the right is a line of discoveries toward the centre of the Galaxy, twenty-six thousand light-years away.

scenes.title: The sky as seen from Earth
scenes.narration: The third view is the sky as seen from Earth. Kepler's field stands out as a dense patch, and stars analysed by this engine are marked in red. Filters underneath narrow the map by how each planet was discovered.

scenes.title: Scored on real stars it never saw
scenes.narration: How good is it? The benchmark page answers with real stars and known answers. Out of nine hundred and ninety labelled Kepler stars, one hundred and eighty-eight were held back and never used for training. On those, the classifier separates planets from everything else with a score of zero point nine eight two, where one is perfect.

scenes.title: Injection and recovery
scenes.narration: Injection and recovery asks a different question: if a planet were there, would the engine find it? Artificial transits are added to quiet real stars and run blind. Strong signals are recovered ninety-eight percent of the time, signals right at the detection threshold half the time, and the faintest almost never, which is how it should be.

scenes.title: Blind, end to end
scenes.narration: The hardest test is the blind run. The pipeline gets only the photometry of ninety held-out stars and must find the period itself. It recovered fifty-five of sixty periods exactly, called twenty-nine of thirty real planets planets, and let only two false positives into the vetting queue. Every star is listed below with its result.

scenes.title: Checked against its acceptance criteria
scenes.narration: The validation page checks the system against its written acceptance criteria. Period, depth, radius, classification and log integrity all pass. Three extended checks run alongside, and the page is honest about the one that misses: eleven of twelve golden-target assertions hold.

scenes.title: New data in, better model out
scenes.narration: Automation lets the engine keep itself up to date. Each cycle pulls the newest TESS objects of interest, downloads more labelled Kepler stars, and retrains once enough have arrived. A new model replaces the current one only if it scores no worse on the held-out stars. It is off by default, and every training run is listed here.

scenes.title: Every stage of every run
scenes.narration: The audit log gathers the records from every run in one place. Filter by level or by pipeline stage, search the messages, and download everything as a single file. Warnings stand out, like the diagnostic flag raised in this run.

focus.label: Filter by level, stage or text
A warning, from a diagnostic flag

scenes.title: Work the physics by hand
scenes.narration: The calculator is an interactive version of the physics. Pick a preset such as WASP-12 b or TRAPPIST-1 e, or move the sliders for the star, the period and the transit depth. The planet's radius, orbit, transit duration and temperature update as you go, and the same scale drawing of the system follows along.

scenes.title: Pipeline defaults in one place
scenes.narration: Settings holds the defaults applied to every new analysis: the outlier threshold, the detrending window, the range of periods to search, and the confidence a signal needs to reach the vetting queue. The acceptance tolerances underneath are fixed, and the storage in use is shown beside them.

scenes.title: The mathematics, written out
scenes.narration: Finally, the method page writes out the mathematics of each stage, from normalisation to the physical parameters, and defines every verdict and every diagnostic flag the engine can raise. Nothing in the pipeline is a black box.

scenes.title: From starlight to a vetted candidate
scenes.narration: That is the Chronos Transit Engine: from raw starlight, to a measured planet, to a decision you can audit, and a place on the map. Thank you for watching.
